study_identification.title: Effects of anterior temporal lobe resection on cortical morphology

study_characteristics.study_objective: To examine the effects of anterior temporal lobe resection (ATLR) on brain morphology using traditional and recently-proposed independent morphological variables.

dataset_name.supporting_text: We also used MR images of crosssectional cohorts of 924 healthy controls, 91 of which were taken together with patients. Specifically, 22 were taken with scanning protocol 1 and 69 with scanning protocol 2 at the NHNN. The remaining 833 controls are subjects from the Nathan Kline Institute (NKI) data set (Nooner et al., 2012).

site_effect_handling.reason: The paper describes using a GAMM to account for site effects (scanning protocol).
site_effect_handling.supporting_text: we performed a correction of these measures based on a normative model of the controls using generalised additive mixed models (GAMM) for each patch on the cortical surface. This correction accounts for differences due to age, sex, and scanning protocol.

site_effect_handling_detail.reason: The paper provides details on the model used for site effect handling.
site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: We trained a model with the formula y ~ s(age) + sex + (1|scanning_protocol) where b is a model coefficient, s is a smooth spline, ε is the error term, and y is one of the measures pT, pA't, or pA'e, using restricted maximum likelihood as the method for smoothing parameter estimation. We used the controls to provide a normative model of age and sex with scanning protocol as a random effect.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: A SurfStat random field theory clustering approach assessed changes across the cortex caused by ATLR.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Anterior temporal lobe resection is followed by widespread morphological changes, detectable with both traditional and novel independent morphological measures.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Surgery had marked effects on all morphological measures. Ipsilateral effects were located in the orbitofrontal and inferior frontal gyri, the pre- and postcentral gyri and supramarginal gyrus, and the lateral occipital gyrus and lingual cortex. Contralateral effects were in the lateral occipital gyrus, and inferior frontal gyrus and frontal pole. Some effects were only visible in the independent variables.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: The study could not decisively determine if morphological change is a sign of atrophy or reorganisation. The analysis was unable to investigate the cingulate cortex with independent morphometrics due to limitations of the method. The study did not test for differences in morphological changes when grouping subjects by language lateralisation.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study suggests that the structural changes found are truly due to the surgery, rather than the progression of the disorder itself. The use of independent morphological measures (K, I, S) can reveal morphological information otherwise concealed in the covariance between the traditional measures.

general_notes.general_notes: The study used a novel set of independent morphological measures (K, I, and S) to assess cortical morphology changes after surgery. The normative model was used to correct for age, sex, and scanning protocol effects, not to calculate patient deviations.
